context_html: By the time the bus finally arrived, Maria <u>waits</u> at the corner for over an hour.
stem_md: Which verb form best completes the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Present-tense 'waits' clashes with the past-tense 'arrived' that anchors the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Had been waiting' places the hour of waiting BEFORE the past arrival — exactly the sequence the sentence describes.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Is waiting' is present tense; the arrival already happened.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Will wait' pushes the waiting into the future, after the bus arrived — backwards.

why_correct_md: An action ongoing **before** a past event takes the past perfect (progressive): *had been waiting*.
why_tempted_md: Each verb form sounds fine alone; only checking it against 'arrived' exposes the clash.
rule_md: Match verb tense to the sentence's time anchors; 'by the time X happened' demands past perfect.

context_html: Yesterday the choir <u>sung</u> the national anthem before the game.
stem_md: Which verb form is correct in this sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Sung' is the past participle and needs a helping verb ('had sung'); alone it cannot serve as the simple past.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Sang' is the simple past of 'sing' — exactly what 'Yesterday' calls for.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Singed' means lightly burned; it is not a form of 'sing'.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Sings' is present tense, clashing with 'Yesterday'.

why_correct_md: Irregular verb: sing → **sang** (simple past) → sung (participle, needs a helper).
why_tempted_md: 'Sung' sounds vaguely past-tense, and the sung/sang pair is easy to swap.
rule_md: Use the simple past form alone; save the participle (sung, swum, begun) for perfect tenses with 'have/had'.

context_html: Of the two routes up the mountain, the eastern trail is the <u>most</u> challenging.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for comparing the two routes?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Most' is the superlative — it needs three or more routes to pick from.
per_choice_rationale.B: Exactly two things compare with the comparative: the eastern trail is the MORE challenging of the two.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'The much challenging' is not idiomatic before a bare adjective.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Very challenging' drops the comparison the sentence explicitly sets up.

why_correct_md: Two items → **comparative** ('more'); three or more → superlative ('most').
why_tempted_md: Superlatives are so common in speech that 'most challenging' sounds natural even for a pair.
rule_md: With exactly two things, use -er/'more'; save -est/'most' for three or more.

context_html: The box of winter clothes <u>were</u> stored in the attic all summer.
stem_md: Which choice makes the subject and verb agree?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Were' agrees with the nearby plural 'clothes', but the subject is the singular 'box'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Have been' is also plural — same trap, plus a tense shift the sentence doesn't need.
per_choice_rationale.C: The subject is 'box' (singular); 'was' agrees with it.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Are' is plural AND present tense; the sentence describes the past summer.

why_correct_md: The verb agrees with the head noun **box**, not with the closer noun in the 'of' phrase.
why_tempted_md: The plural 'clothes' sits right next to the verb, luring the ear toward 'were'.
rule_md: Strip the prepositional phrase to find the true subject before choosing the verb.

context_html: The new policy will <u>affect</u> how employees request time off.
stem_md: Which choice uses the right word for the sentence's meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Affect' is the verb meaning to influence — 'will affect how employees request time off' is already correct.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Effect' as a verb means to bring something about ('effect change'); it cannot take 'how employees request' as its object.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Will affects' stacks a conjugated verb after 'will', which requires the base form.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Will effected' is doubly wrong: wrong word and wrong form after 'will'.

why_correct_md: To influence something = **affect** (verb); the sentence already uses it correctly.
why_tempted_md: The affect/effect pair is so notorious that a correct 'affect' invites second-guessing.
rule_md: Affect = verb (to influence); effect = noun (a result) — and check before you 'fix' what isn't broken.

context_html: The results were consistent <u>to</u> the team's hypothesis.
stem_md: Which choice completes the idiom correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: English pairs 'consistent' with 'with', never 'to'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consistent with' is the standard idiom.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Consistent for' is not an English idiom.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Consistent about' describes a person's habits, not agreement between findings and a hypothesis.

why_correct_md: Idioms are fixed pairings: **consistent with** is the only standard form here.
why_tempted_md: 'To' feels connective, and many adjectives do take 'to' (similar to, equal to).
rule_md: Learn preposition pairings as fixed units — 'consistent with', 'capable of', 'preoccupied with'.

context_html: The volunteer <u>whom</u> organized the food drive received an award.
stem_md: Which pronoun is correct here?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Whom' is an object pronoun, but this pronoun is the SUBJECT of 'organized'.
per_choice_rationale.B: The pronoun performs the verb 'organized', so the subject form 'who' is required.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Which' refers to things; the volunteer is a person.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Whose' shows possession — nothing is being possessed here.

why_correct_md: Subject of the verb → **who**; object of a verb or preposition → whom.
why_tempted_md: 'Whom' sounds more formal, so it gets sprinkled in where 'who' belongs.
rule_md: Test with he/him: 'HE organized the drive' → who; 'the drive was organized by HIM' → whom.

context_html: Lena rehearsed her lines for weeks. <u>Similarly</u>, she froze the moment the curtain rose.
stem_md: Which transition correctly signals the contrast?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' promises more of the same, but freezing on stage contradicts weeks of rehearsal.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'However' names the real relationship: the outcome defied the preparation.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Likewise' makes the same false promise as 'Similarly'.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Therefore' claims freezing FOLLOWED LOGICALLY from rehearsing — backwards.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **contradicts** the expectation the first sets up — that's 'However'.
why_tempted_md: Any transition reads smoothly if you don't test the logical claim it makes.
rule_md: Name the actual relationship (contrast, cause, example, addition) before choosing a transition.

context_html: First, soak the beans overnight. <u>In other words</u>, rinse them and set them to simmer.
stem_md: Which transition fits the step-by-step sequence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In other words' promises a restatement, but rinsing and simmering are NEW steps, not the soaking rephrased.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'For instance' promises an example of soaking — rinsing isn't one.
per_choice_rationale.C: The passage is a sequence of steps; 'Next' moves it to step two.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In contrast' claims the steps oppose each other; they simply follow each other.

why_correct_md: Instructions advance step by step — the transition must mark **sequence**.
why_tempted_md: Restatement transitions sound explanatory, which feels helpful in instructions.
rule_md: In a procedure, use sequence transitions (first, next, then, finally) between steps.

context_html: Ella trained all winter for the marathon. <u>In contrast</u>, she finished in her best time ever.
stem_md: Which transition names the actual relationship between the sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In contrast' promises opposition, but the best-ever finish FOLLOWS FROM the training.
per_choice_rationale.B: The record finish is the outcome of the winter of training — cause and effect.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For instance' promises an example, not an outcome.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'On the other hand' signals the same false contrast as 'In contrast'.

why_correct_md: The second sentence is the **result** of the first — the transition must say so.
why_tempted_md: Any transition reads smoothly if you don't test the logic it claims.
rule_md: Name the real relationship (cause, example, contrast, time) before picking a transition.

context_html: The trail was steep and poorly marked. <u>In fact</u>, the view from the summit repaid every step.
stem_md: Which transition acknowledges the concession the passage makes?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In fact' intensifies what came before; the second sentence pivots away from the complaint instead.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Even so' concedes the hard climb, then asserts the reward despite it — exactly the move the passage makes.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'As a result' claims the great view was CAUSED by bad trail markings.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For example' promises an instance of steepness; a rewarding view isn't one.

why_correct_md: Hardship conceded, reward asserted anyway → a **concession** transition ('even so', 'nevertheless').
why_tempted_md: 'In fact' is a common intensifier, and the sentence pair reads fine until the logic is tested.
rule_md: When sentence two says 'despite that', the transition must carry the concession.

context_html: The library's archive holds thousands of rare maps. <u>Therefore</u>, its oldest map dates to 1502.
stem_md: Which transition best fits what the second sentence does?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' claims the 1502 map is a logical consequence of the archive's size — it isn't.
per_choice_rationale.B: The 1502 map is a specific illustration of the archive's rare holdings — an example.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'However' promises a contrast the sentences don't make.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In conclusion' signals a summary, but the sentence adds a new detail.

why_correct_md: A concrete instance supporting a general claim is introduced with **for example**.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' sounds authoritative, masking that nothing is actually being deduced.
rule_md: General claim followed by a specific instance → an example transition.

context_html: <u>Honey has been harvested for thousands of years.</u> Bees pollinate roughly a third of the crops humans eat, and almond growers truck hives across entire states each spring. Without managed colonies, many orchards would produce almost nothing.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best topic sentence for the paragraph?

choices.label: Beekeepers wear protective suits for good reason.
Honey comes in many colors and flavors.
Bees are essential partners in modern agriculture.

per_choice_rationale.A: The paragraph is about pollination and farming, not the history of honey harvesting.
per_choice_rationale.B: Protective suits never come up — the body is about crops and orchards.
per_choice_rationale.C: Honey varieties are irrelevant to pollination statistics and trucked hives.
per_choice_rationale.D: Every body sentence — the crop share, the trucked hives, the barren orchards — supports bees as agricultural partners.

why_correct_md: A topic sentence must be the claim **every body sentence supports**.
why_tempted_md: Honey feels on-topic because bees make it — adjacency masquerades as relevance.
rule_md: Read the body first; the right topic sentence is the one the details already argue for.

context_html: The essay opens with the image of the lighthouse dark and boarded up. It then recounts the two-year volunteer restoration. <u>Fundraising for the restoration ended in June.</u>
stem_md: The writer wants a conclusion that returns to the essay's opening image of the lighthouse. Which choice accomplishes this?

choices.label: Today the restored beacon sweeps the bay each night, just as it did in 1902.
Many coastal towns face similar budget shortfalls.
The preservation committee will meet again next spring.

per_choice_rationale.A: A fundraising date is administrative housekeeping — it never looks back at the lighthouse.
per_choice_rationale.B: The lit beacon sweeping the bay answers the opening's dark, boarded-up tower — the frame closes.
per_choice_rationale.C: Other towns' budgets point AWAY from this essay's subject entirely.
per_choice_rationale.D: A future meeting is logistics, not imagery.

why_correct_md: A framing conclusion must **revisit the opening image** — dark tower then, lit beacon now.
why_tempted_md: Factually true closers feel legitimate even when they ignore the stated goal.
rule_md: When the stem names the writer's goal, eliminate every choice that doesn't perform it — truth alone doesn't qualify.

context_html: A late frost destroyed half the orchard's trees<u>; consequently,</u> the annual cider festival went on as planned.
stem_md: Which transition matches the relationship between the frost and the festival?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Consequently' claims the festival happened BECAUSE of the frost — the frost worked against it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'For example' would make the festival an instance of frost damage, which it isn't.
per_choice_rationale.C: The festival proceeded DESPITE the destruction — 'nevertheless' carries exactly that defiance.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In addition' stacks the festival on top of the frost as more of the same; they pull opposite ways.

why_correct_md: Setback + outcome-despite-it = **nevertheless**, not a cause-effect transition.
why_tempted_md: 'Consequently' sounds authoritative, and both sentences do describe real events in order.
rule_md: Ask whether the second clause happens because of, despite, or alongside the first — then pick the transition that says so.

context_html: Because the storm had knocked out power across the valley<u> the</u> town meeting moved to the fire hall.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the boundary after the opening clause?

per_choice_rationale.A: A full dependent clause opens this sentence — running it straight into the main clause hides where one ends and the other begins.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma after an introductory dependent clause marks the boundary the reader needs.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon needs independent clauses on BOTH sides; 'Because ... valley' cannot stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.D: A period strands 'Because the storm had knocked out power across the valley' as a fragment.

why_correct_md: An introductory dependent clause is set off from the main clause with a **comma**.
why_tempted_md: Read quickly aloud, the sentence seems to flow fine without any pause.
rule_md: A dependent clause that OPENS the sentence takes a comma before the main clause — 'Because X happened, Y followed.'

context_html: Our biology teacher<u>, Mr. Alvarez,</u> keeps a terrarium of hissing cockroaches behind his desk.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the teacher's name correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: The name merely renames 'our biology teacher', so a PAIR of commas sets it off.
per_choice_rationale.B: An interrupter needs commas on both sides — opening one without closing it splices the name into the verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: Closing the interrupter without opening it makes the comma look like it belongs to the verb phrase.
per_choice_rationale.D: With no commas the name reads as restrictive — as if several biology teachers had to be told apart.

why_correct_md: A renaming appositive is set off by a **pair of commas** — both sides or neither.
why_tempted_md: Only one pause is easy to hear aloud, so a single comma feels sufficient.
rule_md: A nonrestrictive appositive takes commas on BOTH sides; drop both only when the name truly restricts.

context_html: Rex pulled hard, and the <u>dogs'</u> leash slipped from Maya's hand.
stem_md: Which choice makes the possessive correct?

per_choice_rationale.A: The apostrophe after the s marks a plural possessive, but only one dog — Rex — is in the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: One dog owns the leash, so the singular possessive 'dog's' is correct.
per_choice_rationale.C: Without an apostrophe there is no possessive at all — the leash must belong to the dog.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'dogss'' is not a word form in English.

why_correct_md: One owner → apostrophe **before** the s: *dog's*.
why_tempted_md: Plural and possessive forms sound identical aloud, so the written apostrophe placement is easy to miss.
rule_md: Singular owner → 's; plural owners ending in s → s'.

context_html: Whiskers meowed until Maya filled the <u>cats</u> bowl.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the possessive correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: Without an apostrophe, 'cats' is just a plural — nothing shows the bowl belongs to the cat.
per_choice_rationale.B: The apostrophe after the s claims several cats own the bowl, but only Whiskers is in the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: One cat — Whiskers — owns the bowl, so the singular possessive 'cat's' is correct.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'cats's' is not a standard English form.

why_correct_md: One owner → apostrophe **before** the s: *cat's*.
why_tempted_md: Plural 'cats' and possessive 'cat's' sound identical aloud, so the missing apostrophe is easy to overlook.
rule_md: Singular owner → 's; plural owners ending in s → s'.

context_html: Marcus finished the marathon<u>, his</u> sister cheered from the finish line.
stem_md: Which choice best joins the two independent clauses?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: A colon promises that the second clause explains or expands the first; the sister's cheering is a separate event, not an explanation.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon plus 'and,' piles two joiners (and a stray comma) where one is needed.
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon is the standard way to join two closely related independent clauses.

why_correct_md: Two related independent clauses join with a **semicolon** when no conjunction is used.
why_tempted_md: The comma splice reads smoothly aloud, so the error hides in plain sight.
rule_md: Independent clause + independent clause → semicolon, or comma + coordinating conjunction — never a comma alone.

context_html: The recipe calls for three <u>ingredients flour</u>, sugar, and butter.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the introduction of the list?

per_choice_rationale.A: With no punctuation, the list runs into the noun it names — readers can't tell where 'ingredients' ends and the list begins.
per_choice_rationale.B: A colon after a complete statement introduces the list it promises: three ingredients — then names them.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon separates two independent clauses; it cannot introduce a list.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'ingredients'' adds a possessive apostrophe nothing in the sentence calls for.

why_correct_md: A **colon** follows a complete statement to introduce the list it announces.
why_tempted_md: The sentence reads smoothly aloud, so the missing punctuation is easy to skate past.
rule_md: Use a colon — never a semicolon — after a complete clause to introduce a list.

context_html: The judges announced that the three finalists <u>are: a baker from Reno, a chef from Tulsa,</u> and a caterer from Boise.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the introduction of the finalists correctly?

choices.label: are a baker from Reno, a chef from Tulsa,
are: a baker from Reno; a chef from Tulsa;
are; a baker from Reno, a chef from Tulsa,

per_choice_rationale.A: The colon interrupts 'are' and its complement — the clause before a colon must be complete.
per_choice_rationale.B: The list completes the verb directly; no punctuation belongs between 'are' and what the finalists are.
per_choice_rationale.C: This keeps the illegal colon and adds semicolons these short, comma-free items never need.
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon after 'are' cuts the clause off from its own complement.

why_correct_md: 'Are' already introduces the list — **no punctuation** sits between a verb and its complement.
why_tempted_md: Colons DO introduce lists — just not when the words before the colon can't stand alone.
rule_md: Use a colon only after a COMPLETE statement; never right after 'are', 'include', or 'such as'.

context_html: The lifeguard <u>swam</u> toward the struggling swimmer.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the speed of the rescue. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Swam' is accurate but neutral — it says nothing about speed.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Sprinted through the surf' is vivid and fast — exactly the urgency the writer wants.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Made her way' is leisurely, the opposite of urgent.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Eventually paddled' makes the rescue sound slow and reluctant.

why_correct_md: When the stem states the writer's goal, pick the choice that **delivers that goal** most strongly.
why_tempted_md: Accurate-but-bland options like 'swam' feel safe because nothing is wrong with them grammatically.
rule_md: Goal questions are not grammar questions — grade each choice against the stated purpose alone.

context_html: Dr. Okafor became <u>notorious</u> for her groundbreaking vaccine research.
stem_md: Which word carries the connotation the sentence needs?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Notorious' means famous for something BAD — it slanders the research it means to praise.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Infamous' has the same negative charge as 'notorious'.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Renowned' is fame with a positive glow — right for groundbreaking research.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Suspected' implies wrongdoing that the sentence never mentions.

why_correct_md: Denotation is 'famous'; the needed **connotation** is positive → *renowned*.
why_tempted_md: 'Notorious' sounds impressive and vaguely means 'well-known'.
rule_md: Check a word's emotional charge, not just its dictionary meaning, against the sentence's intent.

context_html: The town paper's report on the ceremony noted that the mayor's speech <u>wrapped up</u> with a call for volunteers.
stem_md: Which choice best suits the article's formal register?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Wrapped up' is conversational — out of register in a newspaper report.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Finished off' is just as casual, with a violent shading besides.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Was done' is flat and informal, and weakens the sentence's structure.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Concluded' states the same fact in the neutral, formal register a news report uses.

why_correct_md: Match the diction to the **register** of the surrounding text — formal reporting takes 'concluded'.
why_tempted_md: The informal options are exactly how the sentence would be spoken aloud.
rule_md: Identify the passage's register first; then pick the word that belongs to it.

context_html: In the lab report's discussion section, the experiment's results were <u>super weird</u>, prompting a full review of the method.
stem_md: Which choice best matches the passage's formal tone?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Super weird' is casual slang — jarring inside a formal lab report.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Unexpected' states the same fact in the register a lab report uses.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Totally bizarre' swaps one informality for another.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Kind of strange' keeps the conversational hedge the context forbids.

why_correct_md: Word choice must match the **register** of the surrounding passage — formal here.
why_tempted_md: The informal options are vivid and natural in speech.
rule_md: Check the passage's tone before judging a word: formal context → formal diction.

context_html: The rain finally <u>stopped the players</u> returned to the field.
stem_md: Which choice corrects the fused sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation at all — a fused sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses trades the fused sentence for a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: A period ends the first complete thought and lets the second begin cleanly.
per_choice_rationale.D: The comma after 'players' punctuates nothing — the two clauses are still fused.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a real boundary — here, a **period**.
why_tempted_md: Read quickly, 'the rain stopped the players' parses as one clause, hiding the seam.
rule_md: Find where one complete thought ends and the next begins; mark that seam with a period, semicolon, or comma + conjunction.

context_html: The museum galleries were packed<u>, we</u> headed to the sculpture garden instead.
stem_md: Which choice best repairs the comma splice?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses — this is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Comma + the coordinating conjunction 'so' legally joins the clauses AND names the cause-effect link.
per_choice_rationale.C: Deleting the comma fuses the clauses — no boundary at all.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'However' is not a coordinating conjunction; it would need a semicolon before it.

why_correct_md: Comma + **coordinating conjunction** (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) is a legal clause joiner.
why_tempted_md: 'However' feels like a conjunction, but it's an adverb — the classic splice non-fix.
rule_md: Join independent clauses with comma + FANBOYS, a semicolon, or a period — never a bare comma.

context_html: Although the museum stayed open late<u>. Visitors</u> still missed the final exhibit.
stem_md: Which choice repairs the sentence boundary?

per_choice_rationale.A: The period strands 'Although the museum stayed open late' as a fragment — a subordinate clause cannot stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma joins the introductory 'although' clause to the main clause it modifies.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on BOTH sides; the 'although' clause is dependent.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Although' already subordinates the first clause — adding 'and' doubles up the connectors.

why_correct_md: A subordinate ('although') clause attaches to its main clause with a **comma**, not a period.
why_tempted_md: Reading aloud, the pause after 'late' feels like a full stop.
rule_md: A clause starting with although/because/while cannot stand alone — join it with a comma.

context_html: <u>Walking to school, the rain soaked Jordan's backpack.</u>
stem_md: Which revision corrects the modifier error?

choices.label: As Jordan walked to school, the rain soaked his backpack.
Walking to school, the rain quickly soaked Jordan's backpack.
Walking to school, Jordan's backpack was soaked by the rain.

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Walking to school' has nothing to modify but 'the rain' — and rain doesn't walk.
per_choice_rationale.B: Rewriting the modifier as a clause with its own subject ('As Jordan walked') puts the walker in the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adding 'quickly' changes nothing: the rain is still the one walking.
per_choice_rationale.D: Now the backpack is walking to school — the modifier still dangles.

why_correct_md: A modifier must attach to the noun that actually performs it — give 'walking' its walker, **Jordan**.
why_tempted_md: Every option reads smoothly until you ask WHO is walking.
rule_md: Ask who performs the opening modifier's action; that noun must come immediately after the comma (or be given its own clause).

context_html: The coach praised the team for practicing daily, playing fairly, and <u>that they communicated</u> clearly.
stem_md: Which choice keeps the series parallel?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'That they communicated' breaks the -ing pattern set by 'practicing' and 'playing'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Communicating' matches the two -ing verbs, keeping the series parallel.
per_choice_rationale.C: The infinitive 'to communicate' mismatches the -ing forms.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'They communicated' inserts a full clause where the series expects a single -ing verb.

why_correct_md: Items in a series must share one grammatical form — here the **-ing** form.
why_tempted_md: Each option is grammatical in isolation; only the series pattern exposes the mismatch.
rule_md: Match every item in a list to the form the first items establish (parallel structure).

context_html: The internship taught her to manage budgets, to draft reports, and <u>public speaking</u>.
stem_md: Which choice maintains parallel structure in the list?

per_choice_rationale.A: The noun phrase 'public speaking' breaks the 'to + verb' pattern set by 'to manage' and 'to draft'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'How public speaking works' is a clause, not the infinitive the series expects — and it changes the meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'She learned public speaking' inserts a whole new clause into a series of infinitives.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'To speak in public' matches 'to manage' and 'to draft' — three parallel infinitives.

why_correct_md: Every item in the series must repeat the established form — here, the **infinitive** ('to ___').
why_tempted_md: 'Public speaking' is a perfectly natural phrase on its own; only the series pattern exposes it.
rule_md: Match each list item to the grammatical form the first item establishes.

context_html: The pianist's technique is more polished than <u>the other finalists</u>.
stem_md: Which choice makes the comparison logical?

per_choice_rationale.A: As written, the sentence compares a TECHNIQUE to PEOPLE — apples to orchestra members.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Than the other finalists are' still measures the people, not their technique.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'That of the other finalists' compares technique to technique — like to like.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'The other finalists' were' garbles the grammar and shifts tense mid-comparison.

why_correct_md: Comparisons must pair like with like: technique vs **that of** the others.
why_tempted_md: The shorthand comparison is how people actually talk, so the mismatch hides.
rule_md: When comparing possessions or attributes, add 'that of' / 'those of' so both sides match.

context_html: The committee will meet <u>at 9 a.m. in the morning</u> on Thursday.
stem_md: Which choice cuts the repeated time reference?

choices.label: at 9 a.m. in the early morning

per_choice_rationale.A: 'a.m.' already MEANS morning — 'in the morning' repeats it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Reordering the phrases doesn't remove the repetition.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'At 9 a.m.' states the time once, completely.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Early' adds a third layer to the same redundancy.

why_correct_md: '**a.m.**' contains 'morning'; saying both is saying it twice.
why_tempted_md: The doubled phrase is common in speech, where redundancy aids the listener.
rule_md: Expand abbreviations mentally (a.m. = morning) to catch hidden repetition.

context_html: The twins wore <u>identical matching</u> costumes to the parade.
stem_md: Which choice eliminates the redundant description?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Identical' and 'matching' say the same thing — one of them is dead weight.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Identical' alone carries the full meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: Reversing the order keeps both redundant words.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Identically matching' fuses the two redundancies into one phrase.

why_correct_md: Two words with one meaning → keep **one**.
why_tempted_md: Doubling adjectives feels emphatic, as if two synonyms are stronger than one.
rule_md: Cut any word that repeats what a neighboring word already says.

context_html: Students <u>who are members of</u> the robotics club meet on Tuesdays.
stem_md: Which choice is most concise while preserving the meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Who are members of' is grammatical but spends four words on what one preposition can do.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Students in the robotics club' — same meaning, three words saved.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Happen to belong to' adds hedging the sentence never asked for.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'That are being members of' is both wordier and ungrammatical.

why_correct_md: The ACT rewards the **shortest choice that keeps the meaning** — here, 'in'.
why_tempted_md: The longer relative clause sounds more formal and 'complete'.
rule_md: Try replacing a relative clause with a single preposition; if nothing is lost, the preposition wins.

context_html: The committee reached a <u>consensus of opinion</u> after two hours of debate.
stem_md: Which choice is the most concise without losing meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: A consensus IS an agreement of opinion — 'of opinion' repeats what the word already says.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consensus' alone carries the full meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Shared' stacks a third redundancy onto the phrase.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Unanimous' adds yet another layer of the same idea.

why_correct_md: The ACT rewards the **shortest** option that preserves the meaning — 'consensus' says it all.
why_tempted_md: Longer phrases feel more formal and thorough.
rule_md: Cut words that restate what another word already contains.

context_html: Each morning, she would <u>rise up</u> at dawn to water the garden.
stem_md: Which choice removes the redundant word?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Rise' already means to move up — 'up' repeats it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Rise' alone carries the full meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Upward' is the same redundancy in a longer word.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Get up to rise' says the same thing twice in two ways.

why_correct_md: The direction is **inside the verb**: rising is upward by definition.
why_tempted_md: 'Rise up' is common in speech and song, so it sounds idiomatic.
rule_md: Drop particles that repeat the verb's built-in direction (rise up, descend down, return back).

context_html: <u>Due to the fact that</u> the bridge was icy, the road crew closed it overnight.
stem_md: Which choice trims the wordy opener?

choices.label: In light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Due to the fact that' spends five words doing one word's job.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Because' states the cause directly.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In light of the fact that' is even wordier than the original.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Being that' is both nonstandard and no shorter in spirit.

why_correct_md: **Because** replaces the five-word scaffold with the one word it means.
why_tempted_md: The long phrase sounds official, which reads as 'more correct'.
rule_md: Swap wordy connectors for their one-word equivalents (due to the fact that → because).

context_html: The novel's final chapter<u>, which comes at the end of the book,</u> resolves the mystery.
stem_md: Which choice best trims the redundant clause?

choices.label: , which is located at the book's end,
, coming at the end of the book's final pages,

per_choice_rationale.A: A 'final chapter' by definition comes at the end — the clause adds nothing.
per_choice_rationale.B: Deleting the clause leaves 'The novel's final chapter resolves the mystery' — complete and tighter.
per_choice_rationale.C: Rewording the redundancy doesn't remove it.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'End of the book's final pages' doubles the redundancy it was meant to fix.

why_correct_md: When a clause restates what 'final' already means, the fix is **deletion**, not rephrasing.
why_tempted_md: Rewritten versions look like improvements because they change the words — but not the waste.
rule_md: If a modifier repeats information the noun already carries, delete it entirely.

context_html: The old stone bridge <u>goes over</u> the gorge at a height of ninety meters.
stem_md: Which choice is the most precise description of the bridge?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Goes over' is vague — people go over bridges; bridges do something more specific.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Spans' is the precise verb for a structure stretching across a gap.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Sits over' suggests resting on top of something, not stretching across it.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Happens across' means to encounter by chance — bridges don't do that.

why_correct_md: Precision means the verb built for the job: a bridge **spans** a gorge.
why_tempted_md: 'Goes over' is technically true, and 'true enough' masquerades as 'precise'.
rule_md: Prefer the specific verb over a general verb + preposition when one exists.

context_html: The reason the trail closed <u>is because</u> erosion damaged the footbridge.
stem_md: Which choice corrects the wordy construction after 'reason'?

choices.label: is due to the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'The reason is because' says 'reason' twice — 'because' already means 'for the reason that'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Due to the fact that' swaps one redundancy for five words of another.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'On account of because' stacks two causal phrases — doubly redundant.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'The reason is that' states the cause once, cleanly.

why_correct_md: After 'the reason is', use **that** — 'because' would smuggle in a second 'reason'.
why_tempted_md: 'The reason is because' is extremely common in speech and sounds natural.
rule_md: Pair 'the reason' with 'that'; pair 'because' with a plain clause — never both.
